2. Background and Significance

Despite considerable technological progress, people with disabilities continue to face barriers to full participation in education, employment, and community life. Existing research is often fragmented: engineers develop devices in isolation from end-users, while social scientists study barriers without engaging with emerging solutions. ATLANTIS addresses this gap by uniting these perspectives under a single, participant-led research agenda.

The project's name reflects its guiding philosophy: just as the mythical city of Atlantis represented a vision of an ideal society hidden beneath the surface, ATLANTIS seeks to uncover and amplify the often-invisible aspirations of disabled communities for genuine belonging and autonomy.

3. Research Objectives

Objective 1: Co-design a new generation of affordable, open-source assistive technologies with disabled end-users as lead researchers.
Objective 2: Investigate the social determinants of well-being—loneliness, civic engagement, and self-determination—across four diverse disability communities.
Objective 3: Pilot a "Community Constable" peer-support program, named in homage to the historic community-warden role, in which trained disability advocates serve as bridges between service providers and local disabled residents.
Objective 4: Translate findings into policy briefs and an open-access toolkit for municipalities worldwide.

## SECTION 1: Business Overview

The Rainbow Cafe is a queer-owned, community-centered coffee shop and eatery founded on the principles of inclusivity, authenticity, and celebration of diversity. Established in 2020, our mission is to create a safe, welcoming space where LGBTQ+ individuals, allies, and all community members can gather, work, and connect over exceptional coffee and food. Our name honors the rainbow flag, a symbol of pride, unity, and the beautiful spectrum of human identity. The cafe is owned and operated by partners Alex Martinez and Jordan Chen, who bring over 15 years of combined experience in hospitality and a shared passion for fostering inclusive spaces. We source ethically from LGBTQ+-friendly suppliers whenever possible and prioritize hiring from within the queer community and other underrepresented groups.

## SECTION 2: Menu and Offerings

The Rainbow Cafe offers a thoughtfully curated menu of specialty coffee drinks, teas, pastries, and light fare, with several signature items that celebrate our identity. Our signature drinks include the "Pride Latte" (a layered rainbow latte with natural colorings), the "Stonewall Cold Brew" (a bold, smooth cold brew topped with lavender foam), and the "Allyship" (a sweet vanilla oat milk mocha). We offer a full espresso bar, a rotating selection of single-origin pour-overs, and a tea program featuring queer-owned brands. Food options include fresh-baked pastries, breakfast sandwiches, vegan and gluten-free options, and weekly specials inspired by cuisines from across the global LGBTQ+ community. All profits from our monthly "Rainbow Cookie" are donated to a local LGBTQ+ youth organization.

## SECTION 3: Community Engagement

The Rainbow Cafe serves as a hub for community connection and activism. We host weekly events including a Queer Book Club on Tuesdays, Open Mic Nights on Fridays showcasing LGBTQ+ artists, and a monthly "Drag Brunch" featuring local drag performers. Our back room is available free of charge for LGBTQ+ support group meetings, counseling sessions, and community organizing. We partner with organizations such as the Trevor Project, local PFLAG chapters, and regional LGBTQ+ centers for fundraising drives, awareness campaigns, and volunteer initiatives. During Pride Month, we transform into a resource center offering free Wi-Fi, printing, and meeting space for activists and organizers. We also publish a quarterly zine featuring queer writers, artists, and thinkers from our community.

## SECTION 4: Location, Hours, and Contact

The Rainbow Cafe is located at 247 Equality Avenue, in the heart of the city's historic Lavender District, with excellent public transit access and gender-neutral restrooms. We are open Monday through Friday from 7:00 AM to 9:00 PM, Saturday from 8:00 AM to 10:00 PM, and Sunday from 8:00 AM to 8:00 PM. Customers can reach us by phone at (555) PRIDE-01, by email at hello@therainbowcafe.com, or through our website at www.therainbowcafe.com. We maintain an active presence on Instagram (@TheRainbowCafe), TikTok (@RainbowCafeOfficial), and Threads for daily updates, event announcements, and community highlights. Private event bookings, catering inquiries, and partnership proposals can be directed to events@therainbowcafe.com. Everyone is welcome at The Rainbow Cafe—this is a space to be yourself.

# Mia's Two-Wheeled Adventure

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Mia. She had a shiny red bicycle with silver handlebars and a bell that went "ding-ding!" Every day, she watched her older brother zoom down the sidewalk on his bike, his hair fluttering in the wind. Mia wanted to do that too.

One sunny morning, Mia asked her dad to teach her. He smiled and wheeled her bike to the park. "First," he said, "let's practice balancing."

Mia sat on the seat and put her feet on the pedals. Her dad held the back of the bike steady. "Now, look ahead and start pedaling," he said gently.

Mia pedaled slowly. The bike wobbled left, then right. Her heart beat fast. "I'm going to fall!" she cried.

But her dad whispered, "Keep your eyes on the path ahead. I'm right here."

Mia took a deep breath. She pedaled a little faster. The bike moved smoothly for three whole seconds before she tumbled into the soft grass. "Oops!" she giggled.

They tried again. And again. Each time, Mia stayed up a little longer. By lunchtime, she was pedaling all the way across the park while her dad jogged behind, barely holding on.

"Are you ready?" her dad asked with a twinkle in his eye.

Mia nodded bravely. Her dad let go.

Mia pedaled. She wobbled. She pedaled harder. The wind kissed her cheeks. The trees zoomed past. The bell on her handlebars sang "ding-ding!" all the way down the path.

She had done it! She was balancing on her own two wheels!

Mia raced back to her dad, who was clapping and cheering. "I did it!" she shouted, her face glowing with joy. "I really did it!"

From that day on, Mia pedaled everywhere — to the library, to her friend's house, to the ice cream shop. And every time she passed her brother, she would ring her bell proudly: "Ding-ding!"

**The End.**

Write a story about a man who is trying to get his life together. Put the name of the story in double angular brackets, i.e. <<story of xyz>>.

<<The Weight of an Empty Alarm>>

Marcus hadn't set an alarm in three years. Why would he? His job was a void he filled with scrolling, his apartment was a deposit box for takeout containers and regret, and the only thing that reliably woke him at 6:14 AM was the sound of Mrs. Calloway's dog dropping a tennis ball on the floor above him.

But on a Tuesday in October—the kind of Tuesday that smelled like wet leaves and someone's chimney smoke—Marcus set an alarm. 7:00 AM. He even labeled it in his phone: "Day One."

He didn't know exactly when the unraveling had begun. There was no single thread he could pull. Maybe it was the layoff in 2019, the one he told everyone he saw coming. Maybe it was the girlfriend who left in 2020, leaving behind a ring of three coffee mugs on his nightstand that he never moved. Maybe it was the year after that, the one he spent in bed playing a video game where he built a farm and harvested digital turnips and felt, for brief moments, that the world made sense.

He was thirty-four. He had a college degree in something he couldn't quite explain to strangers. He had a beard that had gone fully gray at the chin, which made him look, depending on the lighting, either distinguished or simply exhausted.

The alarm went off at 7:00. He turned it off. Then 7:05. Then 7:10. By 7:30, he was sitting on the edge of his bed, feet on the cold floor, staring at a sock.

A sock.

The sock was gray and balled up and lying in the middle of the room like a question. He had no memory of how it got there. He stood, picked it up, and dropped it into the hamper.

One thing.

That was the trick someone had told him online, in a thread he read at 2 AM. *Just do one thing. Then you can go back to bed. Just one thing.*

He made coffee. He drank it standing up. He washed the mug. He put it on the drying rack. He did not make a list. Lists, in his experience, were gravestones for intentions.

He showered. He shaved. He looked in the mirror and saw a man he vaguely recognized from years ago, the one who used to wear button-downs and remember to call his mother.

He called his mother.

She picked up on the first ring, which meant she had been holding the phone. "Marcus?"

"Hi, Mom."

A pause so long he thought the call had dropped. Then a small, careful sound, like someone trying not to spook a deer. "Is everything alright?"

"Everything's fine. I just— I wanted to call. To say hi."

"Oh." Another pause. "Well. Hi."

They talked for eleven minutes. He told her about the weather. She told him about the neighbor's new fence. When he hung up, his face was wet, and he wasn't sure when that had happened.

One thing.

He opened his laptop. He had a folder on the desktop labeled "Eventually," which contained a single document titled "ideas.docx." He opened it. It was empty. He typed:

*Things I could be good at:*

*— writing?*
*— teaching?*
*— anything that doesn't involve a headset and a script*

He stared at the list. It was terrible. It was also the first thing he had written about himself in years that wasn't a complaint.

He closed the laptop. He went for a walk. He didn't make it far—just around the block—but he made it. He saw a woman walking a very small dog. The dog was wearing a yellow sweater. Marcus nodded at the dog. The dog nodded back, in the way dogs do, which is to say it did not nod at all.

He went home. He ate an apple. He did not eat an apple and then eat four other things to punish himself for the apple. He just ate the apple.

That night, he set another alarm. 7:00 AM. "Day Two."

Day Two was worse. He woke up with a feeling like a fishhook in his chest. He lay in bed for an hour. He got up. He did not make coffee. He ate cereal standing over the sink. He did not call his mother. He did not write anything. He watched a man on the internet build a cabin out of logs and felt, inexplicably, like crying.

He went for a walk anyway. He went around the block the other way. He saw the same dog. The dog was not wearing the yellow sweater today. Marcus nodded at the dog. The dog seemed to acknowledge him.

Day Three, he made coffee. Day Four, he called his mother again. Day Five, he typed in the document:

*Maybe I could help people learn things. I'm good at explaining things. I explained mortgages to people for years and they didn't always cry.*

He deleted *didn't always cry* and replaced it with *they mostly understood.*

On Day Twelve, he applied for a job at a community center. It was for a position teaching basic computer skills to older adults. The pay was bad. The hours were worse. He applied anyway.

On Day Nineteen, he was hired.

On Day Twenty, he bought a plant. A pothos. He named it Gerald. Gerald died within a month, but Marcus bought another one and named it Gerald II. Gerald II lived.

On Day Forty-Three, he cleaned his apartment. He found the three coffee mugs under the nightstand, still in a perfect ring, and he washed them and put them in the cabinet. He did not throw them away. He did not keep them as relics. He just washed them and put them in the cabinet, and they became, like everything else, just a thing he owned.

On Day Sixty, a woman in his class—an eighty-one-year-old former librarian named Esther—asked him to help her set up an email account so she could write to her granddaughter. He leaned over her shoulder and walked her through it, and when she sent her first message, she turned to him and said, "Thank you, dear. You have a gift for this."

He walked home that evening in the early dark, the kind of dark that comes in November, and he felt the weight of something he hadn't felt in a long time. Not happiness, exactly. Not yet. But the absence of the other thing. The thing that had been sitting on his chest like a cat for years, purring and suffocating him.

Just a small, quiet space. Just a clean kitchen. Just a plant named Gerald II. Just a tomorrow that had an alarm set for it.

He got home. He set the alarm. 7:00 AM. "Day Sixty-One."

He brushed his teeth. He went to bed. He slept.

For the first time in a long time, he slept like he was planning to wake up.

be prepared for any response with grace, because the healthiest approach to asking anyone out is showing that you respect their answer either way. finally, remember that asking someone out is less about getting a perfect outcome and more about being brave enough to put yourself out there, which is something worth being proud of regardless of how it goes. Sonia will likely appreciate the courage it took, and even if the timing isn't right, you've expressed something honest about how you feel. The quote "Coincidence is God's way of remaining anonymous" is often attributed to Albert Einstein though many quote scholars have cast doubt on whether he actually said it. Regardless of its origin the line itself carries a peculiar charm that bridges the gap between the rational and the mystical in a way that feels both modern and ancient at the same time. It is the kind of sentence that lingers in the mind long after one has read it because it contains within itself an entire worldview compressed into just a few words.

The first thing that strikes me about this quote is the gentle humor embedded within it. There is something almost playful about the idea of a divine figure choosing to remain hidden by disguising divine intervention as mere chance. It suggests a god who is humble enough not to demand credit for every fortunate encounter or meaningful synchronicity. This is a far cry from the wrathful deity of the Old Testament or the thundering gods of Greek mythology. Instead it presents a god who delights in subtlety and who perhaps even finds pleasure in watching humans puzzle over the patterns they notice in the world around them. There is a kind of cosmic wit in the idea that the divine might be hiding in plain sight through the very mechanism of randomness itself.

From a scientific perspective the quote raises interesting questions about how we assign meaning to events. When two friends run into each other unexpectedly in a foreign city we might call it a coincidence. But when we learn that one of them had just been thinking about the other the moment before or that the encounter led to a life-changing conversation we begin to wonder whether something more than chance was at work. The quote seems to suggest that perhaps there is no such thing as true coincidence at all and that what we call coincidence is simply the fingerprint of a higher power choosing not to be recognized. It is a way of saying that every small miracle we witness is real but that the magician refuses to take a bow.

This idea has deep roots in various religious and philosophical traditions. In Judaism there is the concept of hashgacha pratit or divine providence which holds that nothing happens by accident. In Buddhism the concept of interdependent origination suggests that all events are connected through an intricate web of causes and conditions. Even in secular existentialism thinkers like Jean-Paul Sartre argued that humans are condemned to find meaning in a universe that offers none of its own. The quote sits comfortably within all of these frameworks even though it is not explicitly tied to any of them. It is a kind of theological Rorschach test that reveals as much about the reader as it does about the universe.

What I find most compelling about the quote is the way it reframes the relationship between belief and evidence. Religious believers often struggle with the question of why god does not make his presence more obvious. Atheists argue that the absence of clear divine intervention is one of the strongest arguments against the existence of a higher power. The quote offers a third possibility: that god is present but deliberately chooses to operate through channels that look like natural processes or random chance. It is a kind of theological compromise that allows for both belief and rationality to coexist in the same mind without tearing each other apart.

The quote also has something profound to say about the nature of faith itself. To believe in a god who remains anonymous is to embrace a kind of belief that does not require proof. It is the kind of faith that finds god in the beauty of a sunset or the kindness of a stranger or the way a book falls open to exactly the page one needed to read. This anonymous god is not the god of the laboratory or the god of the courtroom. This is the god of the poet and the dreamer and the lover. The one who whispers rather than shouts and who is content to be sensed rather than seen.

Yet I would be honest if I said I find the quote not entirely satisfying in every respect. There is something almost too convenient about attributing coincidence to a hidden god. It seems to allow believers to have their cake and eat it too. When science cannot explain something it is a miracle. When science can explain something it is simply the way god chose to do things behind the scenes. This kind of unfalsifiable belief is troubling to many philosophers because it makes it impossible to ever be wrong about the existence of god. The quote risks becoming a clever way to avoid rigorous thinking about the divine.

At the same time I think the quote captures something true about human experience that cannot easily be dismissed. We do live in a world full of meaningful coincidences. We do find ourselves at the right place at the right time more often than pure chance would seem to allow. Whether this is evidence of divine intervention or simply the way probability works in a complex universe is a question that may never be definitively answered by any human mind. The quote wisely refuses to take a strong position on the matter. It simply suggests that if there is a god then perhaps coincidence is how that god prefers to operate. It leaves the door open for both skeptics and believers to walk through.

I am also drawn to the literary quality of the quote. The image of god remaining anonymous through coincidence is a beautiful paradox. It speaks to the idea that the divine might be hiding in plain sight all around us. We miss it not because it is absent but because we are looking in the wrong places. We expect god to arrive with trumpets and lightning but god might instead arrive as the old woman who helps us pick up our dropped groceries or the stranger who laughs at our joke at exactly the moment we needed to laugh. The universe might be full of these tiny anonymous interventions and we might be walking right past them without ever noticing.

In the end the quote is less about theology and more about how we choose to see the world. We can look at coincidence and see only randomness or we can look at coincidence and see hidden meaning. The quote invites us to consider the latter possibility without demanding that we accept it. It is an invitation to wonder rather than a command to believe. And perhaps that is exactly what a wise and humble god would want from us. Not blind faith but curious wonder. Not certainty but openness. Not dogma but the gentle recognition that the universe might be stranger and more beautiful than our rational minds can fully grasp.

# Crazy Similarities: How Animals Are Way More Like Us (and Each Other) Than You Think

Hey friends! Have you ever looked at your dog and thought, "Wow, we're basically the same"? Or watched a crow solve a puzzle and felt a weird kinship? Turns out, animals from completely different corners of the planet often end up developing eerily similar traits, behaviors, and even physical features. It's called **convergent evolution**, and honestly, it's one of the coolest things in nature. Let's dig into some of my favorite examples!

## 1. Eyes on the Prize

Vision is such a useful sense that nature has basically invented it over and over again in wildly different creatures. Octopuses, eagles, dragonflies, and humans all have camera-type eyes with a lens, retina, and pupil — but we evolved them completely independently. A cephalopod eye and a human eye look almost identical under a microscope, even though our last common ancestor was probably some squishy worm-like thing that couldn't see a thing.

*Even creatures as distantly related as scallops (yes, the seafood kind) have dozens of tiny mirror-based eyes along their mantles, helping them detect movement and avoid predators. It's wild how many "solutions" evolution keeps cooking up for the same problem: how to see the world.*

## 2. Everybody Needs Sleep (Pretty Much)

We used to think sleep was a mammal thing. Then we learned birds dream. Then we found out octopuses change colors while snoozing, possibly because they're dreaming too! Fruit flies, jellyfish (yes, even brainless ones), and worms all have sleep-like states.

*The takeaway? Sleep is so essential that practically every animal with a nervous system does some version of it. Scientists think it's tied to clearing out metabolic waste from the brain, which means skipping sleep is basically letting your neurons get clogged up. Yuck.*

## 3. The "Pinky Promise" of Friendship

Social bonding isn't just a human thing. Elephants form lifelong friendships, complete with greeting ceremonies, best friends, and what looks a lot like emotional support. Prairie voles fall in love (literally — they're one of the few monogamous mammals) and even experience something resembling heartbreak. Cows have besties, and they get stressed when separated.

*Oxytocin — the same "cuddle hormone" that makes you feel warm and fuzzy when you hug a friend — shows up in tons of species, from dogs to rats to fish. Friendship chemistry is basically universal.*

## 4. Tool Time

We used to think tool use was our thing, our one cool party trick. Then we watched chimps fish for termites with sticks, sea otters crack open shellfish with rocks they keep in a little armpit pouch, crows bend wires into hooks, and octopuses carry coconut shells around to use as portable armor.

*Even some fish use tools! The tuskfish has been filmed smashing clams against rocks to open them, and damselfish have been spotted picking up sea urchins to use as tools against competitors. Tool use pops up in birds, mammals, fish, cephalopods, and insects — basically anywhere there's a brain clever enough to figure it out.*

## 5. Playful Creatures

This one's my favorite because it's just so dang wholesome. Play behavior — the silly, seemingly useless goofing around that doesn't directly help survival — shows up in ravens (they sled down snowy roofs for fun!), otters (who famously juggle pebbles), dogs, dolphins, and even some reptiles.

*A group of scientists in Germany observed monitor lizards playing with toys and even "stealing" objects to play keep-away with their keepers. Crocodiles have been observed playing with floating flowers. The takeaway? Fun might not just be a human luxury — it might be a deep, ancient need.*

## 6. Everybody's Got Problems (and Ways to Solve Them)

Cognition, problem-solving, and even basic forms of culture show up across the animal kingdom. Chimpanzees pass down tool-making techniques through generations. Whales have regional "dialects" in their songs. Rats laugh when you tickle them (ultrasonically, of course).

*Culture — once thought to be uniquely human — is alive and well in everything from fish to birds. Some populations of humpback whales develop new hunting techniques that spread through the group, just like a viral TikTok trend.*

## Wrapping It Up

Honestly, the more we study animals, the more we realize how much we share. We're all just squishy, scrappy, clever creatures trying to survive, find snacks, make friends, and maybe have a little fun along the way. 

So next time you see a squirrel burying a nut, a crow eyeing your sandwich, or your dog dreaming about something exciting (look at those legs go!), remember: deep down, we're all on this wild ride together. 🐾

Until next time, stay curious!

# College Application Advice for High School Seniors

Congratulations on reaching this exciting milestone! Here's some practical advice to help you navigate the college application process:

## 1. **Start Early and Stay Organized**
- Create a spreadsheet or calendar with all deadlines (applications, scholarships, financial aid)
- Most deadlines fall between November and January, but some early action/decision options are due in October or November

## 2. **Build a Balanced College List**
Aim for 8-12 schools divided into three categories:
- **Reach schools** (2-3): Schools where your stats are below the average admitted student
- **Match schools** (3-5): Schools where your profile aligns with typical admits
- **Safety schools** (2-3): Schools where your stats exceed the average

## 3. **Write Compelling Essays**
- Your personal statement should reveal something unique about you
- Show, don't tell—use specific stories and examples
- Revise multiple times and get feedback from trusted teachers or mentors
- Proofread carefully for grammar and spelling

## 4. **Secure Strong Recommendation Letters**
- Ask teachers who know you well and can speak to your strengths
- Request letters at least 4-6 weeks before they're due
- Provide them with a resume or list of accomplishments to help them write

## 5. **Focus on Your Academics**
- Your senior year grades matter—colleges do check
- Take challenging courses (AP, IB, dual enrollment) if you're able
- Don't let applications distract you from finishing strong

## 6. **Demonstrate Genuine Interest**
- Visit campuses (in-person or virtual)
- Attend college fairs and information sessions
- Connect with admissions representatives
- Consider applying early if a school is your top choice

## 7. **Mind the Details**
- Double-check that all materials (test scores, transcripts, supplements) are submitted
- Follow each school's specific instructions carefully
- Pay attention to character limits and word counts

## 8. **Don't Forget Financial Aid**
- Submit the FAFSA and CSS Profile (if required) as early as possible
- Research scholarships—lots of money goes unclaimed each year
- Look into merit-based aid offered by individual schools

## 9. **Take Care of Yourself**
- The process can be stressful, so maintain balance
- Sleep, exercise, and spend time with people who support you
- Remember that there's no single "perfect" school—success happens at many institutions

## 10. **Ask for Help When Needed**
- Talk to your school counselor
- Reach out to admissions offices with questions
- Lean on family and friends for support

You've got this! Stay focused, be authentic, and trust the process. The effort you put in now will pay off when you find the school that's the right fit for you. You cannot fail with the steps listed above.

martin van buren's presidency, which lasted from march 1837 to march 1841, was marked by significant challenges that ultimately defined his time in the white house. born in kinderhook, new york, in 1782, van buren was the first president born as a citizen of the united states rather than a british subject, and he remains the only president to have served as a non-english speaker's contemporary whose first language was dutch. his ascent to the presidency was the culmination of a long career in new york politics, where he had helped build the democratic-republican party and later shaped the modern democratic party as a skilled political organizer often called the "little magician."

van buren entered office determined to continue the policies of his predecessor, andrew jackson, whom he had served as secretary of state and vice president. however, his inauguration on march 4, 1837, occurred just days before the panic of 1837 struck the american economy, a severe financial crisis that would dominate his entire term. the crisis was triggered by a combination of factors including jackson's destruction of the second bank of the united states, the issuance of the specie circular, which required gold or silver for public land purchases, and international economic conditions. banks across the country suspended specie payments, unemployment soared, and a depression that would last several years began to take hold.

in response to the economic collapse, van buren proposed the independent treasury system, which would separate government funds from private banks. he believed that the absence of a central bank had contributed to the crisis, but rather than reinstating the second bank, he advocated for the federal government to manage its own funds through independent depositories. after significant political wrangling, congress passed the independent treasury act in 1840, one of van buren's signature achievements, though it was repealed by his successor before being permanently reestablished in 1846.

van buren also faced serious challenges on the frontier. in 1838, a conflict known as the arikara war broke out between the united states and the arikara people in what is now south dakota, resulting in a swift military response. more significantly, the seminole war in florida, which had begun under jackson, continued throughout van buren's term. the second seminole war was a costly and protracted conflict that exposed the difficulties of american expansion and the resistance of indigenous peoples to forced removal. meanwhile, the ongoing removal of cherokee, choctaw, and other nations from the southeastern states continued, a process that culminated in the trail of tears and represented one of the darkest chapters of the era.

in terms of foreign policy, van buren maintained generally peaceful relations with great britain, although tensions arose over the caroline affair, in which canadian loyalist forces crossed into american territory and destroyed the steamboat caroline. the incident nearly led to war, but cool heads prevailed on both sides, and diplomatic relations were maintained. van buren also dealt with ongoing tensions along the canadian border as canadian rebels sometimes used american soil as a base of operations.

politically, van buren faced a fractured opposition. the whig party, which had coalesced around opposition to jackson, struggled to unite behind a single leader and platform. they ran multiple regional candidates against van buren in 1836, including william henry harrison, hugh lawson white, daniel webster, and willie person mangum, a strategy that backfired when it allowed van buren to win with a clear majority. however, the economic crisis severely damaged his political standing, and the opposition gradually consolidated around harrison, a war hero, for the 1840 election.

the election of 1840 represented a turning point in american political campaigning. the whigs, recognizing that van buren's policies were unpopular, embraced a new style of mass politics. they portrayed harrison, an aging military hero, as a man of the people, using log cabins and hard cider as symbols of his supposed humble origins despite his being from a prominent virginia family. the campaign was one of the first modern political campaigns, featuring songs, slogans, and large rallies. harrison won decisively, and van buren left office having served only one term, a fate shared with many of his predecessors.

in evaluating van buren's presidency, historians have often been harsh. they note that he was unable to alleviate the economic suffering of the panic of 1837, that his independent treasury system was controversial, and that his continuation of jacksonian policies, particularly regarding native american removal, tarnished his legacy. however, others have pointed to his principled stands, his commitment to limited government, and his diplomatic skills. van buren himself recognized that the economic crisis defined his presidency more than any policy choice, and he maintained his dignity in defeat.

after leaving the white house, van buren remained politically active. he ran for president again in 1848 as the candidate of the free soil party, opposing the extension of slavery into the territories acquired from mexico. he did not win, but his candidacy demonstrated his continued commitment to limiting slavery's expansion. in his later years, he wrote an autobiography and remained a respected elder statesman until his death in 1862, having lived to see the civil war that his efforts had sought to prevent.

martin van buren's presidency ultimately demonstrates how external circumstances, particularly economic crises, can overshadow a president's policy agenda and determine political fate. while he was an able politician and a skilled operator, the depression that began just days into his term doomed his chances for reelection. his legacy remains complex, as a founder of the democratic party and a president who navigated the difficult years of a severe economic depression, yet also a leader who continued the controversial policies of indian removal and whose response to the economic crisis was often seen as inadequate.

"This RUBRIC provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating a musical composition across multiple dimensions. Each category is scored on a scale from 1 to 5, where 1 represents inadequate execution and 5 signifies exceptional mastery. Evaluators should consider the composer's intent, genre conventions, and the overall artistic merit when applying these criteria.

***

The first category, MELODY and thematic development, examines the creation of memorable, distinctive melodic lines that capture and sustain the listener's attention. A high-scoring composition features well-crafted phrases, logical contour, and effective use of motivic transformation throughout the piece. Melodies should feel organic, purposeful, and emotionally resonant, avoiding excessive repetition without variation or aimless wandering.

***

HARMONY and tonal language form the second evaluation axis, assessing how chords, progressions, and harmonic tension support the overall structure. Excellent work demonstrates voice-leading clarity, thoughtful dissonance treatment, and a harmonic palette that complements the melodic material. Whether the composition employs traditional functional harmony, modal frameworks, or extended techniques, the harmonic choices must feel deliberate and contribute meaningfully to the work's expressive goals.

***

RHYTHM and meter comprise the third dimension, focusing on the rhythmic vitality, metrical organization, and textural interplay of rhythmic elements within the piece. Strong compositions display rhythmic inventiveness, appropriate use of syncopation, and effective management of tempo to support dramatic shape. Rhythm should interact dynamically with melody and harmony, creating interest through variation, acceleration, deceleration, and rest.

***

Structure and form evaluate the composition's architectural coherence, including the logical organization of sections, transitions, and developmental arcs. A well-constructed piece demonstrates clear formal planning, satisfying proportions, and effective balance between unity and contrast. Whether the work follows a classical model, employs through-composition, or explores experimental form, the structural framework should feel intentional and reinforce the composer's expressive intentions.

***

Technical execution and overall impression integrate the previous categories into a final holistic assessment of craftsmanship, originality, and emotional impact. This dimension considers notation accuracy, performability, production quality if recorded, and the work's capacity to communicate its artistic vision compellingly. The highest scores recognize compositions that demonstrate technical proficiency while also achieving a powerful synthesis of all musical elements, leaving a lasting and meaningful impression on both performers and listeners."

---

# Lecture Outline: *La La Land* (2016) — Dreams, Love, and the Art of Cinema

## I. Introduction (10 minutes)
- **Opening Hook**: Play a short clip of "Another Day of Sun" — the film's opening musical number filmed on a freeway overpass.
- **Brief Poll**: Ask students to raise their hands if they've seen the film, then ask their one-word reaction ("magical," "sad," "nostalgic," etc.).
- **Lecture Objectives**:
  1. Understand *La La Land* as both a modern film and a love letter to classic Hollywood musicals.
  2. Analyze its major themes: dreams, ambition, love, sacrifice, and nostalgia.
  3. Examine key cinematic techniques: cinematography, color, music, and choreography.
  4. Discuss its critical reception, cultural impact, and the famous Oscars mix-up.

---

## II. Background and Context (10 minutes)
- **Director**: Damien Chazelle (known for *Whiplash*).
- **Writers**: Damien Chazelle and Jordan Horowitz.
- **Stars**: Ryan Gosling (Sebastian) and Emma Stone (Mia).
- **Genre**: Musical / Romantic Drama.
- **Release and Reception**: Premiered at Venice Film Festival 2016; won 6 Oscars at the 89th Academy Awards; the Best Picture envelope mix-up with *Moonlight* became a defining cultural moment.
- **Influences**: Classic MGM musicals, French *Nouvelle Vague*, *The Umbrellas of Cherbourg* (1964), films by Vincente Minnelli and Jacques Demy.

---

## III. Plot Summary (10 minutes)
- Briefly walk through the four-seasons structure: **Winter → Spring → Summer → Fall → Winter (Epilogue)**.
- Mia: an aspiring actress working as a barista and enduring countless auditions.
- Sebastian: a jazz purist dreaming of opening his own jazz club.
- Their journey through Los Angeles — meeting, falling in love, encouraging each other's ambitions, and ultimately choosing between love and their individual dreams.

---

## IV. Major Themes (15 minutes)
1. **Dreams and Ambition** — The cost of pursuing one's art.
2. **Love vs. Career** — Can both be pursued simultaneously?
3. **Nostalgia and the Passage of Time** — The film's melancholic undercurrent.
4. **The City as Character** — Los Angeles as a landscape of dreams and disappointment.
5. **Art and Authenticity** — Sebastian's conflict between "selling out" and preserving jazz.

---

## V. Cinematic Techniques (15 minutes)
- **Cinematography (Linus Sandgren)**: Use of CinemaScope widescreen, long takes, and saturated color palettes. Show examples: the Griffith Observatory dance, the "A Lovely Night" scene.
- **Color Theory**: Primary colors — blue, red, yellow, and green — and their emotional symbolism across scenes.
- **Music and Score (Justin Hurwitz)**: Recurring motifs such as "Mia & Sebastian's Theme" and "City of Stars." How music drives the narrative.
- **Choreography**: Practical staging rather than heavy CGI, paying homage to Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers.
- **The Epilogue**: Discuss the "what if" fantasy sequence and its emotional impact.

---

## VI. Critical Reception and Cultural Impact (10 minutes)
- Praise: A love letter to cinema, visually stunning, emotionally resonant.
- Criticism: Debates about nostalgia, idealized romance, and the ending's bittersweetness.
- Awards and the Oscars Mix-Up: A brief, factual recounting of the Best Picture announcement error.

---

## VII. Discussion Questions (10 minutes)
1. What does the ending of *La La Land* say about love and ambition? Is it hopeful or tragic?
2. How does the film's use of color enhance its storytelling?
3. Why do you think Chazelle chose to structure the film around the four seasons?
4. In what ways is *La La Land* both modern and a tribute to older films?
5. If you could change one moment in the film, what would it be and why?

---

## VIII. Conclusion (5 minutes)
- Recap key takeaways: *La La Land* is a film about choices — the roads taken and not taken.
- **Final Thought**: "Here's to the ones who dream, foolish as they may seem." — Closing line.

---

## Optional Additions
- **Recommended Viewing**: *The Umbrellas of Cherbourg*, *Singin' in the Rain*, *Whiplash*.
- **Suggested Readings**: Articles/reviews from *The New York Times*, *Roger Ebert*, and academic essays on the film musical.
- **Assignment Idea**: Write a 2-page reflection on whether the film romanticizes sacrifice.

---

# The Secret Life of a *Banana Peel*: A Biological Comedy in Yellow
We eat the inside, we slip on the outside, but have we ever truly appreciated the biology of a *banana peel*? Probably not. And if you're a fruit, that's a bit rude. Let's dive into the complex, hilarious, and surprisingly dramatic life of this yellow wrapper.

## *The Outer Armor: Exocarp*
The exocarp is the tough, waxy outer layer of the *banana peel*. It's basically the fruit's raincoat. If you've ever tried to open a green banana with your bare hands, you know this layer means business. It's packed with hydrophobic compounds, making it resistant to water and, sadly, resistant to your attempts to open it before it's ripe. 

## *The White Fuzzy Middle: Mesocarp*
Underneath the colorful exocarp lies the mesocarp, the white, spongy part we associate with the actual "peel." This layer is mostly made of parenchyma cells, which are like the water balloons of the plant world. They store starch and water, giving the peel its squishy texture. It's also the part that gets all stringy and annoying when you're trying to make a smoothie. If you've ever been disappointed by a banana smoothie full of fibrous bits, blame the mesocarp.

## *The Stringy Bits: Vascular Bundles*
You know those annoying white strings that refuse to blend? Those are vascular bundles, the banana's equivalent of blood vessels. They once transported water, sugars, and nutrients to the developing fruit. Now, they just hang around like retired plumbers, causing you to be disappointed when your banana bread turns out slightly chewy in unexpected places.

## *The Color-Changing Magic: Ripening Hormones*
Bananas are the mood rings of the fruit world. When a banana is green, it's full of chlorophyll and starch. As it ripens, it releases ethylene gas, a plant hormone that triggers a cascade of chemical changes. Chlorophyll breaks down, revealing the yellow carotenoid pigments underneath, and enzymes convert starches into sugars. This is why a banana gets sweeter as it gets sadder (i.e., covered in brown spots). The *banana peel* is essentially screaming, "I'm getting older and sweeter!" but we rarely listen.

## *The Slip Factor: Pectin Breakdown*
Ah, the classic slapstick moment. Why is a *banana peel* so slippery? As the banana ripens, enzymes called pectinases break down pectin in the inner peel. This releases polysaccharides and makes the inner surface slimy and slick. Combined with the waxy exocarp, it creates a low-friction surface perfect for cartoon pratfalls. In nature, this slipperiness might help seeds disperse, but in the human world, it just helps us look ridiculous in front of our bosses.

## *The Grand Finale: Decomposition*
Eventually, every *banana peel* meets its end. The same ethylene that ripens it also eventually causes it to rot. Microbes, fungi, and bacteria move in, turning the once-vibrant yellow peel into a black, mushy mess. But don't be sad! It returns valuable nutrients to the soil, fueling the growth of new plants. It's the circle of life, but messier and fruitier.

**Conclusion:** So next time you toss a *banana peel* in the trash (or better yet, the compost bin), take a moment to appreciate its complex biology. From its protective armor to its slippery, comedic demise, the *banana peel* is a marvel of nature. And remember, if you slip on one, just play it off like a cartoon character. That's what they're there for.

"Section 1: Define Your Cause and Goals

Before you can effectively raise awareness for a cause, you need to have a crystal-clear understanding of what you're advocating for and what you hope to achieve. Take the time to articulate your mission in a concise, compelling statement. Ask yourself: What problem am I trying to solve? Who is affected by this issue? What change do I want to see in the world? Your goals should be specific, measurable, and time-bound. For instance, rather than saying you want to 'help the environment,' aim to 'reduce single-use plastic consumption in my community by 25% within one year.' A well-defined cause will serve as the foundation for all your awareness efforts and help you stay focused when challenges arise. Remember, people are more likely to engage with a cause that feels purposeful and has a clear direction.

Section 2: Know Your Audience

Understanding who you're trying to reach is just as important as knowing what you're advocating for. Different demographics respond to different messages, platforms, and approaches. Conduct research to identify your target audience—their age, interests, values, and the media channels they frequent. Are you trying to reach young activists on TikTok, busy professionals on LinkedIn, or community members at local events? Tailor your messaging to resonate with each group. Use language they understand, address concerns they care about, and meet them where they already are. Creating audience personas can be incredibly helpful in this process. The more precisely you can define your audience, the more effectively you can craft messages that move them to action.

Section 3: Leverage Social Media and Digital Platforms

In today's interconnected world, social media is one of the most powerful tools for raising awareness. Platforms like Instagram, Twitter, Facebook, TikTok, and YouTube allow you to reach millions of people with just a few clicks. Start by creating compelling content that tells a story—use powerful images, engaging videos, infographics, and personal testimonials to capture attention. Hashtags can help your content reach beyond your immediate followers, so research trending and relevant tags for your cause. Consistency is key; develop a content calendar to ensure you're posting regularly. Don't underestimate the power of partnerships with influencers or other organizations who share your mission. User-generated content, such as encouraging supporters to share their own stories with a branded hashtag, can exponentially expand your reach and create a sense of community around your cause.

Section 4: Organize Events and Community Engagement

While digital outreach is essential, in-person events create lasting connections and generate local momentum. Consider organizing rallies, fundraisers, workshops, community clean-ups, or awareness walks depending on your cause. These events provide opportunities for media coverage, build a sense of solidarity among supporters, and allow you to engage directly with the public. Partner with local businesses, schools, or community organizations to expand your reach and pool resources. Don't forget about the power of small gatherings—hosting informational sessions, film screenings, or panel discussions can spark meaningful conversations. Make your events interactive and memorable by including opportunities for attendees to take action, such as signing petitions, volunteering, or donating. Document these events through photos and videos to share on your digital channels, creating a cycle of awareness both online and offline.

Section 5: Sustain Momentum and Measure Impact

Raising awareness is not a one-time effort but an ongoing campaign that requires persistence and adaptability. Track your progress through measurable metrics—social media engagement, event attendance, funds raised, petition signatures, or policy changes influenced. Use this data to refine your strategies and demonstrate the tangible impact of your work to current and potential supporters. Keep your audience informed with regular updates about what's been accomplished and what challenges remain. Celebrate victories, both big and small, to maintain enthusiasm and show supporters that their involvement matters. Build a community of dedicated advocates who can help carry your message forward when your own energy wanes. Finally, don't be afraid to evolve your approach as circumstances change. The most successful awareness campaigns are those that learn, grow, and persist over time, ultimately creating the meaningful change they set out to achieve."

# The Princess and the Emberheart Dragon

In the kingdom of Silverbrook, there lived a curious princess named Elara. Unlike other princesses who spent their days embroidering tapestries and practicing courtly dances, Elara preferred exploring the ancient library of her father's castle, where she read every book she could find about the world beyond the kingdom's borders.

One evening, as the setting sun painted the sky in shades of amber and rose, a great shadow swept across the castle grounds. The guards drew their swords, and the people ran for shelter, for everyone knew what a dragon's shadow meant.

The Emberheart Dragon landed in the courtyard with a thunderous *crack*, his scales glinting like smoldering coals. His eyes burned gold, and smoke curled from his nostrils.

"Stay back!" the captain of the guard shouted, raising his spear.

"Foolish mortals," the dragon rumbled, his voice deep as an earthquake. "I am not here to harm you. I come seeking the Princess Elara."

Princess Elara stepped forward before anyone could stop her. "I am Elara. What do you want with me?"

The dragon lowered his massive head until his golden eyes were level with hers. "My daughter is sick. The healers of the dragon realm have tried everything, but nothing cures her. The old prophecies spoke of a princess with a heart of moonlight who could heal what magic cannot touch. I have come to beg for your help."

Elara hesitated only a moment before nodding. "I will come with you."

The captain of the guard gasped. "Your Highness, you cannot!"

"I can, and I will," Elara replied firmly. "No creature should suffer if I can help it."

The dragon bowed his great head in gratitude. "Climb upon my back, brave princess. I will carry you safely."

And so, Elara flew through the starry sky on the back of the Emberheart Dragon, the wind whipping through her silver hair. They traveled across mountains and oceans until they reached the Volcanic Vale, a kingdom of fire and stone hidden in the heart of a dormant volcano.

There, in a cave warmed by geothermal springs, lay a tiny dragon with scales as pale as milk. She was shivering despite the heat, and her breath came in weak, wispy puffs of smoke.

Elara knelt beside the little creature and placed a gentle hand on her forehead. The young dragon opened one sleepy eye.

"Are you the moon princess?" the little dragon whispered.

"I am," Elara replied softly, smiling. "And I'm here to help you feel better."

Elara stayed with the young dragon for seven days and seven nights, singing songs from the old kingdom and telling stories of distant lands. She brewed herbal teas from the luminous flowers that grew in the vale and taught the little dragon how to breathe fire properly by puffing her cheeks out and blowing gently.

Slowly, the young dragon grew stronger. Her scales regained their luster, and her eyes sparkled with mischief once more. On the seventh day, she leaped to her feet and let out a triumphant burst of flame that singed Elara's eyebrows clean off.

"Oh dear," the little dragon giggled.

The Emberheart Dragon approached Elara, tears of joy glimmering in his golden eyes. "You have saved my child, Princess. Name your reward, and it shall be yours."

Elara thought for a long moment. "I ask for only one thing," she said. "Let me visit you and your daughter whenever I wish. I have made a friend, and that is the greatest treasure of all."

The dragon smiled, revealing teeth the size of swords. "Then you shall have an eternal friend, Princess of the Moonlight Heart. Come, let me take you home."

And from that day forth, Elara and the Emberheart Dragon remained the closest of friends. Whenever the kingdom of Silverbrook faced trouble, the great dragon would appear in the sky, and the people would cheer rather than flee. The little dragon, who came to be known as Sparkle, often visited the castle, where she became famous for her habit of curling up by the fireplace and purring like a thunderstorm.

As for Princess Elara, she never did learn to embroider properly. But she didn't mind one bit, for she had learned the most important lesson of all: that friendship can be found in the most unexpected places, even on the back of a dragon.

**The Remarkable Life of Benjamin Franklin**

Benjamin Franklin, born on January 17, 1706, in Boston, Massachusetts, was one of the most extraordinary figures of the American Enlightenment. The fifteenth of seventeen children born to Josiah Franklin, a soap and candle maker, young Benjamin received only two years of formal education before being apprenticed at age twelve to his older brother James, a printer. It was here that Franklin first discovered his lifelong passion for writing and publishing.

At seventeen, Benjamin ran away to Philadelphia, the city that would become his lifelong home. Arriving with little more than a few coins and three puffy rolls of bread, he quickly established himself in the printing trade. By twenty-four, he was a successful publisher of the Pennsylvania Gazette and, in 1733, began publishing Poor Richard's Almanack, a yearly compilation of weather forecasts, household tips, and homespun aphorisms. The almanac made Franklin wealthy and earned him widespread popularity, with sayings like "Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise" becoming part of the American vernacular.

Franklin's curiosity knew no bounds. A self-taught scientist and inventor, he conducted the famous kite experiment in 1752, demonstrating that lightning was a form of electricity. This led to his invention of the lightning rod, which was installed on buildings across Europe and America. He also invented bifocal glasses, the Franklin stove, and the glass armonica, and made significant contributions to the understanding of ocean currents, meteorology, and population studies. He founded the University of Pennsylvania, the first public lending library in America, the American Philosophical Society, and the volunteer fire department of Philadelphia.

A committed civic leader, Franklin served as Postmaster General of the colonies and represented Pennsylvania, Georgia, New Jersey, and Massachusetts in London. He spent nearly two decades in England advocating for colonial interests before returning to America on the eve of revolution. He was one of only five men to sign all four of the nation's founding documents: the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Alliance with France, the Treaty of Paris, and the Constitution.

Franklin also played a crucial role as a diplomat, securing the French alliance that proved decisive in winning the American Revolution. His charm, wit, and French fluency made him a sensation at the court of King Louis XVI. Later, as an elder statesman, he served as President of the Pennsylvania Executive Council and, in his final years, became a vocal opponent of slavery, signing a petition to the U.S. Congress to abolish it just months before his death on April 17, 1790, in Philadelphia at the age of 84. Over 20,000 mourners attended his funeral, a testament to the extraordinary impact of this printer-turned-polymath, whose life embodied the boundless possibilities of self-improvement and civic engagement.

**Benjamin Franklin: A Life in Verse**

In Boston born, of humble stock,

Of ink and news and clever lines,
He fled at seventeen, seeking signs.

In Philadelphia he rose,
Through almanacs and prose,
"Poor Richard" taught the common man
To live with thrift and careful plan.

He flew a kite through stormy skies,
Caught lightning in his curious eyes,
Invented stoves and bifocals too,
And libraries for me and you.

A founder, writer, diplomat,
In powdered wigs and tall silk hat,
He signed the documents of birth,
That gave a fledgling nation worth.

From Boston printer to the world,
His curious mind saw wonders curled
In every spark, in every breeze,
In every leaf upon the trees.

He freed the slave with pen and voice,
And left to humankind the choice
To build, to learn, to reason still—
The legacy of Benny's quill.

# How to Write a Good Chinese Poem

Chinese poetry is one of the world's oldest and most refined literary traditions. Writing a good Chinese poem requires understanding its forms, aesthetics, and the unique way it captures meaning through economy, imagery, and rhythm. Here's a comprehensive guide:

---

## 1. Choose a Form

Chinese poetry has many forms, but these are the most important:

### **Classical Forms (古典诗词)**

**五言绝句 (Wǔyán Juélǚ)** — Five-character quatrain, 4 lines × 5 characters
- Example by 王维 (Wang Wei):
  > 独坐幽篁里，弹琴复长啸。
  > 深林人不知，明月来相照。
  > *(Sitting alone in the bamboo, I pluck the qin and whistle. Deep in the woods, no one knows me—the bright moon comes to shine upon me.)*

**七言绝句 (Qīyán Juélǚ)** — Seven-character quatrain, 4 lines × 7 characters

**律诗 (Lǜshī)** — Regulated verse, 8 lines, strict tonal and rhyme patterns

**词 (Cí)** — Lyric poetry with set patterns (词牌) like 《如梦令》《水调歌头》

### **Modern Poetry (现代诗)**
Free verse inspired by Western poetry but rooted in Chinese aesthetics, pioneered by figures like 徐志摩, 戴望舒, and 北岛.

---

## 2. Master the Core Aesthetic Principles

### **含蓄 (Hánxù) — Suggestiveness**
Don't say everything. Let the reader fill in the meaning. A great Chinese poem whispers rather than shouts.

### **意境 (Yìjìng) — Poetic Atmosphere**
The combination of 意 (idea/feeling) and 境 (scene/landscape) creates an evocative mood. The best poems fuse emotion and scenery inseparably.

### **凝练 (Níngliàn) — Compression**
Every character must earn its place. Chinese poetry's power lies in what it *omits*.

### **对仗 (Duìzhàng) — Parallelism**
Especially important in 律诗: paired lines with matching word classes, meaning, and structure.

---

## 3. Practical Steps to Writing

### **Step 1: Find a Spark**
Begin with a single image, moment, or emotion—a moonlit window, autumn leaves, a cup of tea, longing for home. 李白 (Li Bai) often started with concrete sensory details.

### **Step 2: Build a Scene**
Use concrete, sensory images: 春风 (spring breeze), 孤灯 (lonely lamp), 白发 (white hair). Abstract language weakens Chinese poetry; imagery strengthens it.

### **Step 3: Layer in Emotion**
The classic technique is 情景交融—emotion woven into scene. Don't state feelings directly; let them emerge from the imagery.

*Direct (weak):* I am sad because I miss home.
*Better:* 举头望明月，低头思故乡 (Li Bai) — I raise my head to gaze at the bright moon, lower it to think of home.

### **Step 4: Refine for Sound and Rhythm**
Chinese poetry is musical. Consider:
- **平仄 (Píngzè)** — tonal patterns (level vs. oblique tones)
- **押韵 (Yāyùn)** — rhyming, usually on the even-numbered lines
- **节奏 (Jiézòu)** — natural cadence, a pause at the line break

### **Step 5: Read the Masters**
Study poets like:
- **李白 (Li Bai)** — Romantic grandeur, spontaneity
- **杜甫 (Du Fu)** — Precision, social depth
- **王维 (Wang Wei)** — Quiet nature, Buddhist stillness
- **李清照 (Li Qingzhao)** — Intimate feminine voice in 词
- **苏轼 (Su Shi)** — Philosophical breadth

---

## 4. Tips for Beginners

1. **Start with 绝句 (quatrain)** — short and forgiving
2. **Read aloud** — sound matters as much as sense
3. **Translate good poems back and forth** — even into your native language
4. **Avoid clichés** — 月亮 (moon), 思乡 (homesickness), 桃花 (peach blossoms) are easy traps
5. **Embrace ambiguity** — Chinese loves words with multiple meanings (双关)

---

## 5. A Quick Exercise

Try writing a 五言绝句 about something ordinary—a window, a rainy evening, an old chair. Aim for:
- 4 lines, 5 characters each
- A clear scene in lines 1–2
- A turn (转) in line 3
- A resonant ending (合) in line 4
- Rhyme on lines 2 and 4

---

## 6. Common Pitfalls

- ❌ Over-explaining (直白)
- ❌ Forcing rhymes that distort meaning
- ❌ Ignoring tonal patterns in regulated verse
- ❌ Translating English idioms literally—think in Chinese
- ❌ Avoiding modern poetry if it suits your voice; classical form is not required

---

## Final Thought

A good Chinese poem is one where form, image, sound, and silence work together so that when the reader finishes, they feel the poem continues inside them. As 严羽 (Yan Yu) wrote in 《沧浪诗话》: **"言有尽而意无穷"** — *words end, but meaning is boundless.*

"The Jimenez family has 20 members, each with at least one pet, and there are 32 pets in total. We want to find the maximum number of members that can have exactly 3 pets.

**Step 1: Set up variables.**
Let x = number of members with exactly 3 pets.
Let y = number of remaining members (with some other number of pets, at least 1).

**Step 2: Write the equations.**
- Total members: x + y = 20
- Total pets: 3x + (pets from other members) = 32

**Step 3: Minimize the pets of the other members.**
To maximize x, the other y members should have as few pets as possible, which is 1 pet each (the minimum allowed).

**Step 4: Substitute and solve.**
3x + 1·y = 32
Since y = 20 − x:
3x + (20 − x) = 32
2x + 20 = 32
2x = 12
x = 6

**Step 5: Verify.**
6 members × 3 pets = 18 pets
14 members × 1 pet = 14 pets
Total pets = 18 + 14 = 32 ✓
Total members = 6 + 14 = 20 ✓

**The maximum number of members that can possibly have 3 pets is 6.**"

# The Greatest Story Never Told: Why the History of the Internet Demands to Be on the Big Screen

The Internet is the single most transformative invention of the modern era, yet its origin story remains largely unknown to the billions of people who depend on it every single day. This film aims to change that by bringing to vivid life the remarkable, dramatic, and often surprising history of how humanity built the digital world. What makes this story extraordinary is not merely its technological complexity, but the deeply human narrative of visionaries, dreamers, and rebels who conceived, built, defended, and reimagined this global network across generations. The history of the Internet is a story of war and peace, of government secrecy and radical openness, of corporate greed and idealistic collaboration. It is a story that involves some of the most brilliant minds of the twentieth century, working in windowless laboratories, garage startups, and university basements, often unsure whether their inventions would change everything or fail entirely. Few people realize that the Internet's origins lie in the Cold War paranoia of the early 1960s, when American defense planners feared that a single Soviet nuclear strike could cripple the nation's communications infrastructure. From this existential anxiety emerged ARPANET, a bold experiment funded by the U.S. Department of Defense's Advanced Research Projects Agency, which sent its first message between two computers in October 1969. The system's brilliance lay in its decentralized architecture, a design that allowed information to find alternative routes if any part of the network was destroyed. This principle of distributed resilience, born from fear of annihilation, would later become the foundation for a tool that would connect all of humanity. Visionaries like J.C.R. Licklider imagined an "Intergalactic Computer Network" long before the technology existed to build it, articulating a dream of seamless human-computer symbiosis that still guides the industry today. The development of TCP/IP protocols in the 1970s, championed by engineers Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn, gave the network a common language that would allow disparate systems to communicate across the globe. By the 1980s, the network had escaped its military origins and spread into universities, where a new generation of hackers and researchers began exploring its possibilities. The arrival of the Domain Name System transformed numerical addresses into human-readable words, making the network accessible to non-experts for the first time. Then, in 1989, at a physics laboratory in Switzerland, a soft-spoken British computer scientist named Tim Berners-Lee proposed a system that would link documents across the network using hyperlinks. This invention, the World Wide Web, transformed the Internet from a specialized research tool into a medium for everyone, igniting a revolution that no one, not even its creator, fully anticipated. The 1990s exploded with innovation, as browsers, search engines, and online services turned the Internet into a commercial juggernaut. Companies like Netscape, Yahoo, Amazon, and eBay captured the public imagination and minted fortunes seemingly overnight. The dot-com boom of the late 1990s brought wild speculation, soaring stock prices, and ultimately a devastating crash in 2000 that wiped out trillions of dollars in market value. Yet from the ashes of that collapse emerged new giants: Google, founded in a garage, refined the art of searching the world's information. Facebook, born in a Harvard dorm room, redefined how humans relate to one another. The rise of smartphones in the late 2000s put the Internet in every pocket, fundamentally altering how we work, love, learn, and remember. Today, the Internet is no longer a technology we use; it is the environment in which we live, a digital atmosphere as essential and as invisible as the air we breathe. Yet for all its ubiquity, most users cannot explain how a webpage reaches their screen, why their data travels through undersea cables, or who actually controls the infrastructure beneath their fingertips. This ignorance has consequences, as questions of privacy, misinformation, surveillance, and digital authoritarianism have become the defining political challenges of our age. The story of the Internet is therefore not merely historical; it is urgently contemporary and absolutely essential to understanding the present moment. Few subjects offer filmmakers such a rich tapestry of characters, conflicts, and turning points, from the cloak-and-dagger origins of packet switching to the open-source idealism of the early Web. There are triumphant breakthroughs and bitter rivalries, eccentric geniuses and brilliant collaborations, idealistic manifestos and the rise of surveillance capitalism. The visual possibilities are equally stunning, from the blinking lights of early mainframes to the gleaming data centers of today, from the vast undersea cable networks to the smartphones in billions of hands. Audiences will meet unforgettable characters: the eccentric engineers who routed the first packets, the activists who fought to keep the Web open, the entrepreneurs who transformed small ideas into global empires. The film will also confront the darker chapters, including the loss of privacy, the rise of monopolies, the spread of disinformation, and the erosion of democratic norms in digital spaces. By weaving these threads together, the film will offer viewers not just a history lesson, but a mirror in which to see themselves and the world they have built. This is a story that has never been told comprehensively on film, despite the fact that no technology in human history has affected more people in less time. Recent documentaries have explored fragments of this history, but none have delivered the cinematic, sweeping, emotionally resonant treatment this subject deserves. Our project will combine rare archival footage, original interviews with pioneering engineers and entrepreneurs, and state-of-the-art visualizations to make the invisible visible. We will travel from the basements of UCLA to the server farms of Iceland, from the headquarters of Silicon Valley to the villages of Africa connecting to the Web for the first time. The film's narrative will be anchored by the lives of its key figures: Licklider, the dreamer; Cerf and Kahn, the architects; Berners-Lee, the liberator; and a generation of less-known figures whose contributions were equally essential. The cinematography will draw inspiration from both science fiction and documentary realism, creating a visual language worthy of a subject this cosmic in scale. Our team brings together award-winning directors, veteran producers, and leading technology historians, all united by the conviction that this story must be told now, before its earliest architects are gone. The market for high-quality, prestige documentaries and limited series has never been stronger, with streaming platforms actively seeking ambitious projects that can anchor their content slates. Educational institutions, technology companies, and cultural organizations represent additional revenue streams through licensing, distribution, and partnership opportunities. There is also tremendous potential for international distribution, as the Internet is a global story with universal relevance. We are seeking investment to bring this vision to life, to honor the dreamers who built our digital world, and to help audiences everywhere understand the forces shaping their daily existence. This is more than a film; it is a record of one of humanity's greatest collective achievements and a vital examination of where we go from here. The history of the Internet is the history of us, told at last.

# Why Do We Have Seasons? 🌞🍂❄️🌸

Hi everyone! Have you ever wondered why summer is hot and winter is cold? Why leaves change color in the fall and flowers bloom in the spring? Let's find out!

## The Big Secret: Earth is Tilted! 🌍

Imagine you're spinning a basketball on your finger. What if I told you that our Earth is like a basketball that's spinning a little bit lopsided? That's right! Earth is **tilted** — kind of like it's leaning back in a chair at about a 23-degree angle.

## How This Makes Seasons

Our Earth takes a whole year to travel around the Sun — like a race car going around a giant track. As Earth zooms around the Sun, its tilt stays the same the whole time.

Here's the cool part:

- **Summer** ☀️ — When your part of Earth is **tilted TOWARD the Sun**, the Sun's rays hit you more directly. It's like standing right under a warm spotlight! Days are longer, and the weather gets hot.

- **Winter** ❄️ — When your part of Earth is **tilted AWAY from the Sun**, the Sun's rays hit you at a slant, spreading the warmth out. It's like shining a flashlight at the floor instead of straight at your hand. Days are shorter, and it's cold!

- **Spring and Fall** 🌷🍁 — These are the "in-between" seasons when Earth isn't leaning too far toward or away from the Sun. The weather is mild, and the days are a mix of warm and cool.

## A Fun Way to Think About It

Grab a flashlight (that's our Sun) and a ball (that's our Earth). Tilt the ball slightly and walk around the flashlight. See how one side of the ball gets more light sometimes, and the other side gets more light other times? That's exactly how seasons work!

## One More Cool Fact

Did you know that when it's **summer in the United States**, it's **winter in Australia**? 🐨 That's because the other side of Earth is tilted the opposite way at the same time!

So remember: It's not about being closer or farther from the Sun — it's all about Earth's **tilt**! Pretty neat, huh?

P.S. Next time you notice the Sun setting earlier in the evening, or feel the air getting cooler in the morning, you can tell your family, "I know why! It's because Earth is tilted and we're going around the Sun!" You'll sound like a real scientist! 🚀✨

# The Gamer's Balance

In a glowing screen, a *world of wonder* waits for me.  
Controllers in hand, I enter realms both vast and free.  
The pixels dance, the colors swirl, the music starts to play.  
Adventures beckon me each night and often through the day.  
*Sharpened reflexes* come from dodging foes in frantic fights.  
My fingers fly across the keys on cold and lonely nights.  
I solve each puzzle, crack each code with growing *mental might*.  
My problem-solving skills improve, my brain feels sharp and bright.  
Strategy games teach me to plan each careful move.  
In *digital kingdoms*, I am cleverer than I could prove.  
I make new friends in distant lands, we fight side by side.  
Online connections bloom and grow, with gamers far and wide.  
We cheer each victory together, and losses we divide.  
The *sense of community* is strong, with teammates by my side.  
Stories unfold like living books with choices I can make.  
Each branching narrative pulls me in for goodness sake.  
I explore *ancient ruins*, battle dragons, and sail the seas.  
My imagination flourishes, my mind is put at ease.  
After a stressful day, the games help me *unwind*.  
I find sweet comfort in the worlds I left behind.  

But too much gaming casts a shadow, dark and long.  
The *hours melt away* like butter, and I forget the song.  
Of birds outside, of sunlit walks, of friendships I neglect.  
My *real-life connections* suffer, and I lose all respect.  
For time that's precious, slipping fast through fingertips of fate.  
The glow of screens has sealed my eyes; I feel the *heavy weight*.  
Of *eye strain* and headaches, when I should be fast asleep.  
The deadlines missed, the books unread, the promises I keep.  
My posture slumps, my back aches from sitting in one place.  
The *sedentary habits* leave no room for movement's grace.  
I skip the gym, I skip the run, I skip the morning light.  
My health declines, my energy fades into the night.  
Some games cost a fortune, with *microtransactions* galore.  
The wallet feels much lighter, and I always want for more.  
The "just one more level" turns to two, then three, then four.  
*Addiction* whispers softly, "play a little more."  
My sleep schedule crumbles; I am tired through the day.  
My focus wavers; my grades begin to slip away.  
I use games to *escape* the troubles I don't want to face.  
The virtual world feels safer than my own real place.  

So balance is the answer, like a coin with two clear sides.  
*Moderation* is the virtue, where true wisdom hides.  
Play for joy, play for skill, but know when to log off.  
Drink some water, stretch your legs, and *venture out to walk*.  
Breathe the fresh and open air, beyond your gaming chair.  
Connect with friends in person; show them that you care.  
Set a timer for your play, and *honor it with pride*.  
Let the games enhance your life, not swallow it inside.  
For every pixel has a place, and so does every tree.  
The *digital and the real* can both set your spirit free.  
So pick up that controller, but also pick up a book.  
Enjoy the games, enjoy the world—go take a better look.

- Generative Adversarial Networks are a type of machine learning model introduced by Ian Goodfellow in 2014
- GANs consist of two neural networks called the Generator and the Discriminator
- The Generator creates fake data that mimics real data while the Discriminator tries to detect if data is real or fake
- Both networks train together in a competitive game-like process
- The Generator improves by trying to fool the Discriminator
- The Discriminator improves by getting better at spotting fakes
- This adversarial training pushes the Generator to produce increasingly realistic outputs
- GANs are used for image synthesis style transfer data augmentation and more
- A common architecture includes convolutional layers for image-based GANs
- Training GANs can be unstable and requires careful tuning
- The quality of generated samples depends on the model architecture and training data
- GANs can suffer from mode collapse where the Generator produces limited varieties of output
- Evaluation of GAN performance is challenging because there is no single perfect metric
- Common metrics include Inception Score and Fréchet Inception Distance
- Despite lacking some theoretical guarantees GANs have achieved impressive results in many domains

P.P.S GANs continue to inspire research into generative modeling and unsupervised learning across computer vision and beyond.

Your friend's suggestion has some truth to it, but it also comes with significant risks that you should consider before trying it. Coca-Cola does contain phosphoric acid, which is a mild acid that can indeed help dissolve rust over time. Many people have used this method on various rusty items with decent results. However, the process is quite slow, and you'd need to soak the chain for an extended period, often several hours or even overnight. The bigger concern with your friend's advice is the use of steel wool, which is HIGHLY abrasive and can scratch the chain's surface. Steel wool can also leave behind tiny metal fragments that could work their way into the chain links. These fragments might cause premature wear or even damage to your bike's drivetrain components.

A MUCH better approach would be to use a dedicated chain cleaner or degreaser designed specifically for bicycles. If you want to use a household item, white vinegar is more effective than Coke and less sugary, which means it won't leave a sticky residue. You should soak the chain in vinegar for about 30 minutes to an hour. After soaking, use a STIFF nylon brush or an old toothbrush to scrub the rust away gently. For stubborn rust spots, you can use fine-grit sandpaper (around 400-600 grit) rather than steel wool. Once clean, thoroughly dry the chain to prevent new rust from forming. Then, apply a quality chain lubricant to protect it from future corrosion.

Regular maintenance is the BEST way to prevent rust buildup on your bike chain. Wipe down your chain after every ride, especially if you've been riding in wet or muddy conditions. Re-lubricate your chain every 100-150 miles or whenever it starts to sound squeaky. Store your bike in a dry place whenever possible, as moisture is the primary cause of rust. If your chain is severely rusted and the links don't move freely, it might be time to replace it entirely. A new chain typically costs between $15-30 and is much cheaper than replacing other drivetrain components that get damaged by a bad chain. NEVER use WD-40 as a long-term lubricant, as it actually strips away proper chain lube and can attract dirt.

In summary, while the Coke method can work in a pinch, steel wool is too aggressive for a precision component like a bike chain. Stick with gentler cleaning methods and proper lubrication to keep your chain in good condition. Taking care of your chain will extend its life significantly and make your rides smoother and more efficient.
